Pushing the Limits of Low-Bit Optimizers: A Focus on EMA Dynamics

Cong Xu Affiliation: East China Normal University Correspondence to: congxueric@gmail.com    Wenbin Liang Affiliation: East China Normal University Affiliation: Tencent Youtu Lab    Mo Yu Affiliation: WeChat AI, Tencent    Anan Liu Affiliation: Machine Learning Platform Department, Tencent TEG    Ke-Yue Zhang Affiliation: Tencent Youtu Lab    Lizhuang Ma Affiliation: East China Normal University    Jianyong Wang Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Jun Wang Affiliation: East China Normal University Correspondence to: wongjun@gmail.com    Wei Zhang Affiliation: East China Normal University Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Correspondence to: zhangwei.thu.2011@gmail.com
Abstract

The explosion in model sizes leads to continued growth in prohibitive training/fine-tuning costs, particularly for stateful optimizers which maintain auxiliary information of even 2x the model size to achieve optimal convergence. We therefore present in this work a novel type of optimizer that carries with extremely lightweight state overloads, achieved through ultra-low-precision quantization. While previous efforts have achieved certain success with 8-bit or 4-bit quantization, our approach enables optimizers to operate at precision as low as 3 bits, or even 2 bits per state element. This is accomplished by identifying and addressing two critical challenges: the signal swamping problem in unsigned quantization that results in unchanged state dynamics, and the rapidly increased gradient variance in signed quantization that leads to incorrect descent directions. The theoretical analysis suggests a tailored logarithmic quantization for the former and a precision-specific momentum value for the latter. Consequently, the proposed SOLO achieves substantial memory savings (approximately 45 GB when training a 7B model) with minimal accuracy loss. We hope that SOLO can contribute to overcoming the bottleneck in computational resources, thereby promoting greater accessibility in fundamental research.

Keywords: 
Optimization, Quantization, LLM

https://github.com/MTandHJ/SOLO

1 Introduction

The rapid scaling of model sizes has begun to strain the ongoing advancement of AI across various domains (e.g., Computer Vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023), Natural Language Processing (Radford, 2018; GenAI, 2023), and Recommender Systems (Zhai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a)). Fundamental AI research is, regrettably, becoming a luxury beyond the reach of most researchers and teams. Recall that modern optimizers typically consume substantial memory to maintain auxiliary information aimed at optimizing and accelerating convergence. For instance, the commonly adopted Adam(W) optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) necessitates a buffer of 2x model size to track 1st moment (for approximating the signed ‘global’ descent directions) and 2nd moment (for approximating the unsigned the adaptive learning rates). As illustrated in Figure 1, these maintained states account for nearly half of the total memory usage in a standard mixed-precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2018).

Once the optimizer is slimmed down, the saved memory can be reallocated to accommodate a larger model or increased batch size. There are some straightforward hardware-level methods to accomplish this, such as GPU sharding (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) and CPU offloading (Ren et al., 2021); however, these solutions are known to struggle with excessive communication overloads (Wang et al., 2023), and are not easy to use in practice. Low-bit optimizers (Dettmers, 2015), which maintain states at low precision, stand out due to their orthogonality to the model architecture, task, hardware, and the aforementioned distributed algorithms. For example, about 1/8\nicefrac{{1}}{{8}} of the memory overhead is enough for an optimizer if the states are maintained in 4-bit instead of the original 32-bit format. Previous efforts have achieved certain success in 8- or 4-bit quantization (Dettmers et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a), but they just apply regular quantization tricks to minimize the quantization error, overlooking the peculiarities of the optimizer state update. As a result, the existing 4-bit optimizers have a non-negligible performance degradation, not to mention 3-bit or 2-bit precision.

Recall that the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) mechanism with a momentum β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) is widely employed in modern optimizers to update state xx upon received signal zz:

xt+1←β⋅xt+(1−β)⋅zt+1.x_{t+1}\leftarrow\beta\cdot x_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot z_{t+1}.

We demonstrate that some overlooked problems exist when unsigned or signed quantization is directly applied to EMA state updates on the fly:

  • •

    Unsigned EMA update is susceptible to a signal swamping problem (Higham, 1993; Wang et al., 2018b); that is, the state might keep unchanged regardless of the gap between the newly received signal and the current state value. This problem becomes particularly severe when employing a large momentum (β→1\beta\rightarrow 1), where the added value of (1−β)​zt+1(1-\beta)z_{t+1} becomes very small and is thus easily swamped, even when the incoming signal zt+1z_{t+1} is actually large. Since the unsigned EMA update is typically used to estimate adaptive learning rates, the useful adaptivity can no longer kick in once the swamping problem occurs.

  • •

    Signed EMA update is highly susceptible to quantization errors due to the additional burden of sign representation and its direct impact on the update direction. Moreover, these quantization errors inherently increase the gradient noise variance, leading to inevitable slowdowns in convergence and even training collapses.

Thanks to these deeper understandings, we are to develop Stateful Optimizers in ultra-LOw bits (SOLO). To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to point out the feasibility of reducing optimizer precision to as low as 3 or even 2 bits.

  • •

    While standard stochastic rounding (Xia et al., 2020) is the straightforward way to escape from strict signal swamping, it is unfortunately accompanied by high variance when quantifying state values close to zero. In order to achieve robust unsigned state quantization, more quantization levels should be allocated near the zero point rather than evenly distributed levels. Hence, the logarithmic quantization (Oh et al., 2021) with a specific base is adopted. It allows for an exact exponential decay with an easy-to-implement stochastic rounding mechanism.

  • •

    We derive an upper bound for the gradient noise variance when performing low-bit quantization in signed EMA updates. Since too high a gradient variance impairs training (Li et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2024), we hypothesize that an acceptable convergence rate can be achieved if the upper bound can be somewhat controlled. It suggests an adjustment of the momentum value β\beta; for instance, if β=0.9\beta=0.9 performs effectively in 5-bit signed EMA updates already, a reduced value of β≤0.820\beta\leq 0.820 is recommended in the 4-bit scenario for an acceptable gradient noise variance. In practical applications, we offer a table as an empirical reference (see Figure 4).

We apply SOLO to the widely used Adam(W) optimizer, giving two variants operating at ultra-low precision. First, we propose the 4/2-bit Adam(W), which performs 4-bit signed and 2-bit unsigned quantization, respectively. This version is equivalent to a 3-bit Adam(W) optimizer in memory savings but allows more stable performance due to a more balanced bit allocation. Second, we develop a 2-bit Adam(W) optimizer to explore the limits of ultra-low-bit optimizers.

The superiority of SOLO has been demonstrated across various domains: (CV) Swin-T for image classification; (NLP) Transformer-Base for neural machine translation and RoBERTa-Large for natural language understanding; (RS) DCN for click-through rate prediction and HSTU-Large for sequential recommendation. Finally, we validate the effectiveness in giant model training, including (LLM) LLaMA-7B fine-tuning on Alpaca and (LVM) LLaVA-1.5 visual instruction tuning based on CLIP and Vicuna-7B-1.5.

This paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing related work, with a focus on efforts to alleviate the ‘hardware bottleneck’. Subsequently, we delve into the details of low-bit optimizers and systematically analyze the challenges involved, followed by discussions on feasible solutions. In Section 4, we present a comprehensive comparison between SOLO and other low-precision counterparts, supported by extensive empirical analysis. For clarity, preliminaries on quantization methods and detailed theoretical proofs are provided in Appendix.

2 Related Work

2.1 Efficient Architecture and Parallelism

One of the most straightforward approaches is to redesign the base model (Waswani et al., 2017; Radford, 2018; Gu & Dao, 2023), such as replacing the computationally intensive attention mechanism with alternatives like multi-head latent attention (Liu et al., 2024a) or linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), or employing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures (Shazeer et al., 2017). This usually improves both training and inference efficiency but requires extensive engineering validation. There are some more parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques (Han et al., 2024), such as soft-prompt on tuning the input (Li & Liang, 2021) and LoRA on low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2021). Since only a limited number of parameters are involved in training, the required optimizer states can be significantly reduced.

Data and model parallelism have been widely employed for large-scale model training across multi-GPU clusters. Recent studies have identified their limitations in memory reduction, prompting the development of specialized optimization techniques (Seide et al., 2014). For instance, ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) enables efficient partitioning of optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters. Furthermore, ZeRO-Offload (Ren et al., 2021) and ZeRO-Infinity (Rajbhandari et al., 2021) extend this framework by leveraging CPU and NVMe resources, respectively, for enhanced memory utilization. However, these strategies are associated with a non-negligible communication overhead, despite the presence of certain modifications (Wang et al., 2023).

In summary, the aforementioned training strategies are often dependent on specific models or hardware, necessitating additional code refactoring. The low-bit optimizers explored in this study are orthogonal to these approaches and exhibit a broader range of applicability.

2.2 Network Quantization

While model training and inference are typically conducted at full precision (i.e., 32 bits) by default, significant memory savings can be achieved through the application of low-precision quantization (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024b; Frantar et al., 2022). This approach has achieved remarkable success in the inference phase, where the quantization precision can be reduced to as low as 4 (Lin et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025) with minimal performance degradation by ‘smoothing’ the activation outliers. As a result, deploying LLMs on personal computers becomes feasible.

However, this is still difficult to apply to Fully Quantized Training (FQT) in a model-independent manner (Zhou et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2022; Xi et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2023). While FP16/BF16 mixed-precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2018) has been extensively validated, the appropriate approach for lower-precision quantization has yet to be thoroughly established. Indeed, the FP8 mixed-precision training has only recently been realized in giant model training (Liu et al., 2024b). Current 4-bit (Sun et al., 2020) and even 1-bit (Gao et al., 2024) FQT methods remain far from practical due to the significant and unacceptable loss in accuracy.

2.3 Lightweight Optimizers

Lightweight optimizers have garnered increasing attention (Shazeer & Stern, 2018; Dettmers et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2024) as traditional stateful optimizers are memory-intensive. Most alternatives aim to simplify the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) by condensing the 2nd state (Anil et al., 2019), namely the adaptive learning rates on the fly. For instance, Adafactor (Shazeer & Stern, 2018) introduces factored 2nd state estimation, while the recently Adam-mini (Zhang et al., 2024b) observes most entries within a block could share a common 2nd state. In addition, GaLore (Zhao et al., 2024a) attains memory-efficient optimization by conducting state updates in a low-dimensional space. Lion (Chen et al., 2024) relies solely on 1st sign momentum to achieve comparable performance across most tasks.

Although these optimizers are lightweight by design, their generalizability has not been thoroughly validated compared to the widely adopted Adam(W) optimizer. We therefore focus on low-bit optimizers due to their model-, task-, and hardware-agnostic characteristics. They enable seamless deployment following the same procedures as their high-precision counterparts, while substantially reducing the effort required for hyperparameter tuning compared to the aforementioned lightweight optimizers. Moreover, some lightweight optimizers like Adafactor can also benefit from low-bit quantization, further reducing memory consumption. Currently, 8-bit (Dettmers et al., 2022) and 4-bit (Li et al., 2023a) optimizers have been developed, primarily relying on regular quantization tricks such as linear or dynamic exponent mappings. In the following, we analyze how the overlook of the EMA update mechanism hinders the development of ultra-low-bit optimizers.

3 Ultra-Low-Bit Optimizers

It is well known that the auxiliary information maintained by an optimizer contribute substantially to the overall memory cost. For instance, the commonly adopted Adam(W) optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) necessitates a buffer of 2x model size to track 1st moment (for approximating the signed ‘global’ descent directions) and 2nd moment (for estimating the unsigned adaptive learning rates), about 520 GB memory usage for a 65B model. In the following, we first elucidate the effectiveness of the low-bit optimizer for addressing this problem, and then systematically analyze the challenges and corresponding solutions when extending to ultra-low-precision scenarios.

3.1 Quantization and Dequantization in EMA Update

The bb-bit quantization for a high-precision tensor XX aims to map each element x∈Xx\in X to an integer q∈{0,1,…,2b−1}q\in\{0,1,\ldots,2^{b}-1\}. Given the scale factor Δ:=maxx∈X⁡|x|\Delta:=\max_{x\in X}|x|, a majority of quantizers can be unified as a nearest rounding process:

q=Q⁡(x):=argmink=02b−1⁡|xΔ−yk|.\displaystyle q=Q(x):=\mathop{\text{argmin}}\limits_{k=0}^{2^{b}-1}\big|\frac{x}{\Delta}-y_{k}\big|. (1)

where yk,k=0,1,…,2b−1y_{k},\>k=0,1,\ldots,2^{b}-1 are monotonic quantization levels distributed across the interval [0, 1] ([-1, 1]) for unsigned (signed) quantization. For instance, linear quantization is a simple yet effective method, utilizing evenly distributed levels. Intuitively, the resulting quantized value qq implies the normalized value x/Δx/\Delta is closest to the qq-th (indexed from 0) level yqy_{q}. These low-precision integers, along with a full-precision scale factor, can be stored and subsequently utilized to ‘recover’ the high-precision tensor:

x~=Q†​(q):=yq⋅Δ.\displaystyle\tilde{x}=Q^{\dagger}(q):=y_{q}\cdot\Delta.

Compared to the original high-precision tensor, the storage of quantized values benefits from reduced memory requirements, albeit at the expense of introducing some quantization (rounding) errors.

Recall that most recent (Adam-style) optimizers rely on the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for state updates. In the context of low-precision quantization, this process can be divided into three steps:

Dequantization: x~t=Q†​(qt)=yqt⋅Δt,\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{t}=Q^{\dagger}(q_{t})=y_{q_{t}}\cdot\Delta_{t}, (2)
EMA update: x^t+1←β⋅x~t+(1−β)⋅zt+1,\displaystyle\hat{x}_{t+1}\leftarrow\beta\cdot\tilde{x}_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot z_{t+1}, (3)
Quantization: qt+1=Q⁡(x^t+1),\displaystyle q_{t+1}=Q(\hat{x}_{t+1}), (4)

where zt+1z_{t+1} is the received signal at t+1t+1 update. Taking the Adam optimizer as an example, zt+1z_{t+1} corresponds to the gradient gt+1g_{t+1} in the signed state update and the sqaured gradient gt+12g_{t+1}^{2} in the unsigned state update. We emphasize that the signed and unsigned EMA updates typically serve distinct roles in optimizers. Subsequently, we analyze the respective challenges and propose feasible solutions, beginning with unsigned updates to signed updates.

3.2 Quantization for Unsigned EMA Update

3.2.1 Signal Swamping Problem

Recall that the unsigned EMA update is commonly applied in the denominator to estimate adaptive learning rates. Therefore, the primary goal is to ensure that the x^t\hat{x}_{t} closely follow the trend of the ground-truth state xtx_{t}. Unfortunately, for certain quantization levels yiy_{i} with a large radius, the swamping problem (Higham, 1993; Wang et al., 2018b), frequently observed in large-to-small number addition, may arise severely. In this case, the received signal is ‘swamped’ by the current state value, potentially resulting in a constant state, which fundamentally undermines the intended purpose of applying EMA.

Theorem 3.1 (Signal Swamping).

Let yqty_{q_{t}} be the closest level to qtq_{t}, and its radius be defined by

r=12​min⁡{|yqt−yqt−1|,|yqt+1−yqt|}.r=\frac{1}{2}\min\Big\{|y_{q_{t}}-y_{q_{t}-1}|,|y_{q_{t}+1}-y_{q_{t}}|\Big\}.

The quantized state qtq_{t} remains unchanged if

r≥(1−β)⋅|zt+1Δt+1−yqt|+|ΔtΔt+1−1|.r\geq(1-\beta)\cdot\Big|\frac{z_{t+1}}{\Delta_{t+1}}-y_{q_{t}}\Big|+\Big|\frac{\Delta_{t}}{\Delta_{t+1}}-1\Big|. (5)

In other words, if the radius around yqty_{q_{t}} is large enough, the state will keep constant even receiving a quite different signal. Four key factors significantly increase the likelihood of the signal swamping problem:

  • •

    Low precision. A lower precision generally results in a larger radius rr since the entire interval must be covered with fewer quantization levels.

  • •

    Large tensor size. For a larger-size tensor XX quantized as a whole, the scale factor Δ=maxx∈X⁡|x|\Delta=\max_{x\in X}|x| becomes larger, potentially leading to a smaller value of |zt+1/Δt+1−yqt||z_{t+1}/\Delta_{t+1}-y_{q_{t}}|. Moreover, changes from Δt\Delta_{t} to Δt+1\Delta_{t+1} tend to be negligible, further exacerbating this issue.

  • •

    Unsigned EMA update. Note that for the signed state update, the accumulation process incorporates both positive and negative values. This results in a mixed state with a much smaller magnitude compared to the signal itself. In this case, the swamping problem is less severe due to a large |zt+1/Δt+1||z_{t+1}/\Delta_{t+1}| allowed. Conversely, the unsigned EMA update is more prone to signal swamping.

  • •

    Momentum β→1\beta\rightarrow 1. A large momentum β\beta has a direct impact on the swamping problem. Notably, the unsigned EMA state update typically employs a larger momentum (e.g., β=0.999\beta=0.999) compared to the signed EMA update (e.g., β=0.9\beta=0.9), which further exacerbates the issue in the unsigned EMA update.

To summarize,

The impact of signal swamping. The EMA update serves as a dynamic estimation of the expectation 𝔼⁡[zt]\mathbb{E}[z_{t}] when ztz_{t} follows a stationary distribution. Clearly a state undergoing signal swamping cannot be expected to converge to the true expectation value, not to mention the complex state dynamics in practice. In other words, once the swamping problem arises, the cumulative approximation error will inevitably grow to an unacceptable level. To provide a clearer understanding of this impact, we demonstrate several surprising cases associated with two widely adopted quantization methods. As the unsigned EMA state update is most affected, we present the analysis on unsigned quantization and leave a generalized version in Appendix B.

Corollary 3.2.

If Δt+1=Δt\Delta_{t+1}=\Delta_{t} and rt≥2​(1−β)r_{t}\geq 2(1-\beta), the unsigned quantized state qtq_{t} remains unchanged for any zt+1≤Δtz_{t+1}\leq\Delta_{t}. To be specific,

  • •

    For linear quantization, the received signals are swamped by states corresponding to any level when

    β⪆0.999⏟8-bit,0.967⏟4-bit,0.929⏟3-bit,0.833⏟2-bit.\displaystyle\beta\gtrapprox\underbrace{0.999}_{\text{8-bit}},\underbrace{0.967}_{\text{4-bit}},\underbrace{0.929}_{\text{3-bit}},\underbrace{0.833}_{\text{2-bit}}. (6)
  • •

    For dynamic exponent quantization, the received signals are swamped by states corresponding to half of the levels when

    β⪆0.998⏟8-bit,0.966⏟4-bit,0.933⏟3-bit,0.837⏟2-bit.\displaystyle\beta\gtrapprox\underbrace{0.998}_{\text{8-bit}},\underbrace{0.966}_{\text{4-bit}},\underbrace{0.933}_{\text{3-bit}},\underbrace{0.837}_{\text{2-bit}}. (7)

Here ‘⪆\gtrapprox’ omits negligible rounding errors.

Corollary 3.2 depicts an extreme case in which the majority of signals are swamped, causing the corresponding states to remain seemingly constant. The following example, based on synthetic data, provides further empirical evidence without the fixed Δt\Delta_{t} condition.

Example 3.3 (Synthetic uniform signals).

Consider X∈ℝ1000X\in\mathbb{R}^{1000}, where both the initial states and subsequent received signals are independently drawn from a uniform distribution 𝒰⁡[0,1]\mathcal{U}[0,1]. Figure 2 depicts the converged state values after 100 iterations.

It is evident that both linear and dynamic exponent quantization fail to converge to the expected value of 0.50.5 for a slightly large tensor when the momentum parameter β→1\beta\rightarrow 1 is adopted. This also explains why the previous approaches (Dettmers et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a) relied heavily on block-wise quantization. In contrast, the solution proposed below exhibits exceptional robustness, making it more suitable for the unsigned EMA update.

3.2.2 Our Unsigned EMA State Quantization

Stochastic rounding.

The swamping problem would not exist any more if we apply stochastic rounding (Xia et al., 2020) instead of the nearest rounding method used in the Eq. (1). Without loss of generality, for a yk−1≤x/Δ≤yky_{k-1}\leq x/\Delta\leq y_{k}, stochastic rounding suggests

Qs​r​(x):={k−1w.p.yk−x/Δyk−yk−1,kw.p.x/Δ−yk−1yk−yk−1.Q_{sr}(x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}k-1&w.p.\quad\frac{y_{k}-x/\Delta}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}},\\ k&w.p.\quad\frac{x/\Delta-y_{k-1}}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}}.\end{array}\right. (8)

As a result, even receiving a very small signal zt+1z_{t+1}, it could benefit from a non-zero probability, thereby escaping from the swamped state. Unfortunately, this is often accompanied by high variance when quantizing a state value close to zero, as the unsigned EMA state typically appears in the denominator. To be specific, the stochastic rounding in Eq. (8) demonstrates a variance as follows:

Proposition 3.4.

For a 2nd state value yk−1≤x/Δ≤yky_{k-1}\leq x/\Delta\leq y_{k} to be quantized, the corresponding adaptive learning rate has a variance:

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(1x^)=𝒪⁡((Δyk−Δyk−1)2).\mathbf{Var}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{x}}})=\mathcal{O}\bigg(\Big(\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k}}}-\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k-1}}}\Big)^{2}\bigg). (9)

As observed, with the same spacing |yk−yk−1||y_{k}-y_{k-1}|, a higher variance is likely to arise as the value yk−1→0y_{k-1}\rightarrow 0 from the right. To mitigate this issue, more quantization levels should be allocated near the zero point to provide compensation. This justifies that the commonly used linear or dynamic exponent quantization methods may not be well-suited in this scenario, as they fail to adequately account for this consideration.

As shown in Figure 3, we therefore adopt the logarithmic quantization with a specific base α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), where the levels11 1 Notably, unlike the convention, the levels here are arranged in a monotonically decreasing order for the sake of notational simplicity. Nevertheless, the aforementioned conclusions remain valid and applicable. become yk=αk,k=0,…,2b−1y_{k}=\alpha^{k},\>k=0,\ldots,2^{b}-1. In addition, we apply a rounding mechanism slightly different to Eq. (8):

Q⁡(x)\displaystyle Q(x) =Clip​(⌊logα⁡xΔ+ξ⌉,0,2b−1)\displaystyle=\text{Clip}(\lfloor\log_{\alpha}\frac{x}{\Delta}+\xi\rceil;0,2^{b}-1) (10)
≈argmink=02b−1⁡|xΔ⋅αξ−yk|,\displaystyle\approx\mathop{\text{argmin}}\limits_{k=0}^{2^{b}-1}\big|\frac{x}{\Delta}\cdot\alpha^{\xi}-y_{k}\big|,

where ξ∼𝒰⁡[−0.5,0.5]\xi\sim\mathcal{U}[-0.5,0.5] and ⌊⋅⌉\lfloor\cdot\rceil denotes the convergent rounding used in IEEE 754 floating-point operations. This stochastic rounding mechanism is preferred here because 1) It is straightforward to implement, as it eliminates the need to calculate an level-specific probability for each state value; 2) It allows for a exact exponential decay when consecutive zero signals are received, aligning with the real state decay:

Proposition 3.5 (Consecutive zero signals).

For a state value starts with βc​k,c,k∈ℕ+\beta^{ck},\>c,k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, it takes c⋅sc\cdot s iterations to decay to (βc)k+s(\beta^{c})^{k+s} if the subsequent signals z≡0z\equiv 0. For the logarithmic quantization with a base α=βc\alpha=\beta^{c}, the average number of iterations required to decay from (βc)k(\beta^{c})^{k} to (βc)k+s(\beta^{c})^{k+s} is given by

𝔼⁡[(βc)k→Ours(βc)k+s|z≡0]=c​s,\mathbb{E}\big[(\beta^{c})^{k}\xrightarrow{\text{Ours}}(\beta^{c})^{k+s}\big|z\equiv 0\big]=cs, (11)

which aligns with the the real state decay.

It is worth noting that aligning this state decay is of particular value if parameters are partially involved during training. This situation is frequently encountered during the construction of massive embedding tables, which serve as fundamental components in both natural language processing and recommender systems. Because only a subset of embeddings is sampled during each mini-batch training iteration, the resulting gradient tends to be highly sparse. In addition, some operations such as dropout can also result in zero gradients.

The interval [xmin,Δ][x_{\min},\Delta] could be fully covered with both endpoints being exactly achievable, if α=(xmin/Δ)1/(2b−1)\alpha=(x_{\min}/\Delta)^{1/(2^{b}-1)}. However, the minimum value xminx_{\min} is numerically unstable and may potentially act as an outlier, especially for a tensor of large size. Therefore, the final desired base is defined as α=(xp/Δ)1/(2b−1)\alpha=(x_{p}/\Delta)^{1/(2^{b}-1)} with xpx_{p} being the pp-quantile of the entire tensor to be quantized. Empirically, a value of p∈[0.05,0.3]p\in[0.05,0.3] has been found to be effective across various scenarios from small to giant models. Figure 3b illustrates a toy example of 2-bit unsigned logarithmic quantization.

3.3 Quantization for Signed EMA Update

As discussed earlier, the signed EMA state quantization is only minimally impacted by the signal swamping problem due to its signed nature and typically small momentum value β\beta. Nonetheless, it presents two distinct challenges in comparison to unsigned EMA state quantization:

  • •

    Signed quantization must allocate one bit to represent the sign, which inevitably amplifies quantization errors under the same precision constraint.

  • •

    The signed state demonstrates significantly higher sensitivity to quantization errors. A substantial quantization error could potentially reverse the descent direction to an ascent direction, significantly impairing convergence.

As a result, training failures are frequently observed in low-precision quantization, particularly in cases where training begins from scratch. To summarize,

Quantization errors amplify the variance of gradients. Here, we theoretically justify why the signed EMA update is susceptible to quantization errors. Firstly note that the received signal z=gz=g for signed EMA updates represents the stochastic gradient over a mini-batch. Some prior studies (Li et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2024) have demonstrated that reducing gradient variance contributes to the convergence. However, the quantization error can be treated as a component of gradient stochasticity, indeed increasing the variance of gradients.

Theorem 3.6.

Let the maximum radius under bb-bit stochastic quantization be

rmax​(b)=maxk=12b−1​12​|yk−yk−1|.r_{\max}(b)=\max_{k=1}^{2^{b}-1}\frac{1}{2}|y_{k}-y_{k-1}|.

The quantized EMA state update of the stochastic gradient gg is equivalent to a standard EMA state update:

xt+1←β⋅xt+(1−β)⋅g~t+1,x_{t+1}\leftarrow\beta\cdot x_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot\tilde{g}_{t+1}, (12)

where g~t+1\tilde{g}_{t+1} denotes the stochastic gradient with

𝔼⁡[g~t+1]=𝔼⁡[gt+1],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}_{t+1}]=\mathbb{E}[g_{t+1}], (13)
𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[g~t+1]⪅𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[gt+1]+(β1−β​rmax​(b)⋅Δt)2.\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}[\tilde{g}_{t+1}]\lessapprox\mathbf{Var}[g_{t+1}]+\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}r_{\max}(b)\cdot\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}. (14)

Theorem 3.6 suggests that as the spacing between the quantization levels decreases or the momentum hyperparameter β\beta increases, the additional gradient variance is progressively introduced. The former implies that the high gradient variance is almost inevitable in the ultra-low-bit scenario, where large spacing arises due to the insufficient number of levels. Clearly, the breakthrough here does not lie in the design of a quantization scheme. SOLO thus turns to a modified momentum hyperparameter β′\beta^{\prime} to regulate the variance introduced by quantization within an acceptable range. If the model converges properly under bb-bit quantization with a momentum hyperparameter β\beta, we hypothesize that a similar convergence rate can be achieved with a modified combination of (β′,b′)(\beta^{\prime},b^{\prime}) subject to

β′1−β′​rmedian​(b′)≤β1−β​rmedian​(b).\frac{\beta^{\prime}}{1-\beta^{\prime}}r_{\text{median}}(b^{\prime})\leq\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}r_{\text{median}}(b). (15)

It is worth noting that rmedianr_{\text{median}} is adopted in place of rmaxr_{\max} because the ratio of r∗​(b)/r∗​(b′)r_{*}(b)/r_{*}(b^{\prime}) is nearly identical for both the median and maximum radius while the former demonstrates greater stability under ultra-low-bit cases. Figure 4 illustrates the β′\beta^{\prime} allowed for unsigned DE quantization. Empirically, 55-bit quantization is sufficient to maintain accuracy in most fine-tuning scenarios; hence, we adopt the corresponding β′\beta^{\prime} in b=4,3,2b=4,3,2 bits as an alternative to β=0.9\beta=0.9. Nevertheless, the optimal β′\beta^{\prime} should be determined based on practical scenarios. For example, training from scratch is more susceptible to quantization errors in comparison to fine-tuning, and thus a lower β′\beta^{\prime} corresponding to 88-bit should be considered.

3.4 Application: 4/2-bit and 2-bit Adam(W)

Since Adam(W) (Kingma & Ba, 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) is the most widely adopted optimizer for training and fine-tuning, we introduce in detail two SOLO-quantized variants of Adam(W).

  • •

    4/2-bit Adam(W) applys a 4-bit DE quantization to the signed EMA update, while a 2-bit logarithmic quantization, as introduced in Eq. (10), to the unsigned EMA update. Notably, it yields memory savings equivalent to a 3-bit Adam(W) while offering additional advantages: 1) As previously discussed, the signed EMA update is more susceptible to quantization errors and should therefore be allocated more bits if possible; 2) Technically, until the work done, mainstream deep learning frameworks have only provided official low-bit storage up to 8-bit precision. To this end, two 4-bit entries or four 2-bit entries should be packed into a single 8-bit element for storage, whereas such straightforward packing is not feasible for 3-bit representations. In addition, based on Figure 4 and empirical observations, a reduced value of β≤0.820\beta\leq 0.820 for fine-tuning and β≤0.350\beta\leq 0.350 for training from scratch generally ensures a stable training process. In default, we fix the momentum of the signed EMA update at 0.8 for fine-tuning and 0.3 for training from scratch, while keeping the momentum for the unsigned EMA update unchanged.

  • •

    2-bit Adam(W) applies 2-bit quantization to both the signed and unsigned EMA updates, representing the extreme case explored in this study. Note that this implies the 32-bit state values would be quantized into only four levels; the signed state encounters an additional challenge, as one bit must be allocated for sign representation, thereby reducing the effective precision. Analogous to the 4/2-bit Adam(W), unless otherwise specified, we fix the momentum of the signed EMA update at 0.5 for fine-tuning and 0.1 for training from scratch, while keeping the momentum of the unsigned EMA update unchanged. Regarding the pp-quantile used in the tailored logarithmic quantization, we fix p=0.1p=0.1 for simplicity.

Following previous low-bit optimizers (Dettmers et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a), block-wise quantization with a block size of 128 is adopted. This approach splits the entire tensor into blocks and performs quantization separately on each block. However, we emphasize that the developed unsigned logarithmic quantization is robust to the choice of block size, whereas this is not the case for other approaches.

4 Experiments

In this section, we aim to investigate the superiority of SOLO by comparing it with its full-precision counterparts as well as other low-bit alternatives.

Tasks. Since low-bit optimizers are model- and task-agnostic techniques, they are expected to be applicable across a wide range of scenarios. Here, we consider three primary application domains, Computer Vision (CV), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Recommender Systems (RS), to ensure a reliable and comprehensive evaluation. CV and NLP are tasks that attract significant interest from the research community, while RS represents a practical application receiving particular focus from the industrial sector. For each domain, we initially employ some benchmarks that are relatively modest in scale by current standards. In addition, we further investigate the performance of instruction tuning for both Large Language Model (LLM) and Large Vision Model (LVM). Detailed descriptions of the models and datasets are provided in the Appendix C.1.

Baselines. We consider baselines ranging from full-precision to 2-bit optimizers. The 16-bit Adam(W) optimizer is implemented using a standard BF16 format, which has been validated in the large-scale training of DeepSeek-v3 (Liu et al., 2024b). The 8-bit Adam(W) variant (Dettmers et al., 2022) employs the dynamic exponent quantization for both signed and unsigned cases. For the lower-precision 4-bit and 2-bit counterparts, as suggested by (Li et al., 2023a), a modified linear quantization scheme that excludes the zero point is employed for unsigned quantization while keeping the signed dynamic exponent quantization unchanged. For a fair comparison, SOLO and other low-bit counterparts adopt block-wise quantization with a size of 128. However, as demonstrated in Figure , this constraint can be significantly relaxed for SOLO, whereas other approaches are highly sensitive to it.

Implementation details. We implement SOLO-quantized and other low-bit optimizers based on the same PyTorch-based library, torchao22 2 https://github.com/pytorch/ao . Training and fine-tuning protocols strictly follow the official codebase, with the only exception being a modified batch size to accommodate the available GPUs. Most of the results reported below are averaged over three independent runs. Given the robust performance and high computational demands of Swin-T and LLaVA-1.5, we limit our evaluation to a single run. The specific hyperparameter settings are listed in Appendix C.1.

4.1 Overall Comparison

In Table  and , we compare SOLO-quantized 4/2-bit Adam(W) and 2-bit Adam(W) with other low-precision counterparts, covering diverse models, tasks, and training strategies. There are some promising observations:

  • •

    Through the comparisons presented in Table , particularly the results obtained by training from scratch (), it is evident that the original full-precision (i.e., 32-bit) states contain considerable redundancy, allowing a straightforward reduction in precision to 8-bit format. However, this redundancy alone is insufficient to support further reductions to 4, 3, or 2 bits without addressing the aforementioned challenges, resulting in potential training instability or even training failure. Remark that in the original paper (Li et al., 2023a), the 4-bit Adam(W) optimizer achieves competitive performance on the Swin-T training task. The discrepancy may arise from our adoption of a stricter unified block-wise quantization strategy (tensors containing less than 4096 entries are quantized as well) to ensure a fair comparison. Owing to the attention to signal swamping and high variance, SOLO-quantized optimizers are able to achieve comparable performance even in the extreme case of 2-bit quantization.

  • •

    LLM fine-tuning demonstrates a surprising tolerance to quantization errors: no training collapses are observed, and the resulting performance consistently surpasses that of the original base model. However, 8-, 4-, and 2-bit optimizers quantized by previous strategies evidently converge to local optima, making it difficult to believe that they can replace the full-precision AdamW optimizer. The proposed SOLO quantization scheme substantially mitigates this issue, owing to its specific considerations of signal swamping and high gradient variance challenges. The 4/2-bit variant outperforms most low-precision counterparts, with performance on three out of five benchmarks even exceeding that of the half-precision (i.e., 16-bit) AdamW optimizer. Admittedly, fine-tuning with the 2-bit configuration remains highly challenging for large-scale fine-tuning; nonetheless, it still attains performance comparable to that of the 8-bit AdamW optimizer.

  • •

    For visual instruction tuning, the performance degradation caused by quantization errors is negligible until 2-bit representation. This is because the MLP projector that bridges the visual encoder tower (CLIP) and the LLM (Vicuna-7B-v1.5) has already been pretrained in full precision. However, scaling to a fully 2-bit setting remains a significant challenge. Thanks to SOLO’s gradient variance control, the 2-bit quantized AdamW optimizer under SOLO still exhibits competitive performance. It is worth noting that, in some cases, the ultra-low-bit optimizer even outperforms its full-precision counterpart. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact (Zhang et al., 2024b) that grouping elements within a block to share the same adaptive learning rate (i.e., the 2nd moment) may facilitate a better convergence.

  • •

    Note that low-bit optimizers typically incur additional computational overhead, resulting in slightly longer training times. Nonetheless, this overhead could be further reduced by optimizing our implementation with fused operators, as suggested by (Li et al., 2023a). However, the implementation of the specified fused operators demands technical engineering effort, which lies beyond the scope of this work and is left for future work.

4.2 Generalizability

  • •

    Block size. Block-wise quantization has been widely adopted to narrow the numerical range subject to quantization, thereby significantly reducing quantization errors. However, the block size cannot be indefinitely reduced, as each 32-bit scale factor Δ\Delta introduces an additional overhead of 1/4\nicefrac{{1}}{{4}} bits per block. In the case of SOLO, the presence of a buffered logarithmic base incurs the double overhead, amounting to 1/2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} bits per block. Consequently, a block size of 128 is approximately the smallest permissible. Nonetheless, we argue that the proposed logarithmic quantization has remarkable generalizability in this aspect. Figure  compares the results under block sizes of 128 and 2048, where our method significantly outperforms the others. The bottom panel further substantiates the superiority of our approach, as the proposed logarithmic quantization preserves state dynamics that closely resemble those of the original 32-bit AdamW.

  • •

    AdaBelief. Although the results in Table  involve the Adam and AdamW optimizers, it is of interest to examine the generalizability of SOLO to other optimizers that incorporate an EMA update mechanism. Table 1 presents the application of SOLO to AdaBelief (Zhuang et al., 2020), which also demonstrates comparable performance. Remark that SOLO can also be applied to lightweight optimizers such as Adafactor (Shazeer & Stern, 2018). However, the use of FSDP renders the comparison infeasible, as the optimizer states in this case are flattened and partitioned, making the row-wise and column-wise states maintained in Adafactor invalid.

4.3 Empirical Analysis

Some empirical analysis is performed in this part to provide intuitive exposition of SOLO.

  • •

    Modified β1\beta_{1}. We discuss in Section 3.3 the necessity of reducing β1\beta_{1} to regulate the gradient variance introduced by quantization. As shown in Figure , the LLaMA model fine-tuned with 4/2-bit AdamW performs optimally at β1=0.8\beta_{1}=0.8 or 0.90.9, and its performance deteriorates as β1\beta_{1} decreases. Conversely, the performance of the model improves in the 2-bit case and reaches its best near β1=0.5\beta_{1}=0.5. This confirms our theoretical findings and the rationale summarized in Figure 4.

  • •

    Loss curve. As illustrated in Figure 5, the SOLO-quantized 4/2-bit and 2-bit AdamW optimizers demonstrate loss curves closely resembling that of the original full-precision AdamW. In contrast, the 2-bit AdamW that incorporates the quantization approaches proposed in (Li et al., 2023a) exhibits significantly poorer convergence, consequently resulting in consistently inferior performance. In addition, the specialized rounding mechanism introduced in Eq. (10) is essential; otherwise, a deteriorated loss curve would be observed.

  • •

    Logarithmic base. Figure 6 demonstrates how sensitive of SOLO to the choice of logarithmic base α\alpha. Recall that α=(xp/Δ)1/(2b−1)\alpha=(x_{p}/\Delta)^{1/(2^{b}-1)} is determined by the pp-quantile xpx_{p}. When pp is too large (i.e., p→1p\rightarrow 1), more small state values are directly truncated, leading to high-variance learning rates. Conversely, when pp is too small (i.e., p→0p\rightarrow 0), the base choice tends to be an outlier, resulting in unacceptable quantization errors. Fortunately, SOLO exhibits a satisfactory robustness as p∈[0.05,0.3]p\in[0.05,0.3].

5 Conclusion

SOLO is designed to slim down the most memory-intensive component during training, guided by two key principles: (I) Generalizability. Although certain optimizers are lightweight by design, their generalizability has not been thoroughly validated compared to the widely adopted Adam(W) optimizer. SOLO is a model-, task-, and hardware-independent technique, as it is capable of keeping consistent optimization dynamics even after ultra-low-bit quantization. (II) Flexibility. The application of certain distributed algorithms and network quantization approaches demands substantial engineering effort. On the contrary, SOLO can be seamlessly applied to most Adam-style optimizers without the need to retune hyperparameters such as the learning rate or weight decay.

Previous efforts have achieved certain success in 8-bit or 4-bit quantization; however, they violate the generalizability principle. On the one hand, they overlook the signal swamping problem frequently arised in unsigned EMA updates, leading to poor approximation to the true state dynamics. In other words, their application essentially changes the nature of the original optimizer in the ultra-low-bit case, thereby failing to guarantee that performance is maintained. On the other hand, signed quantization approaches can not be directly scaled to ultra-low precision owing to the increased gradient variance; otherwise, training failures are likely to occur. SOLO addresses these two challenges through comprehensive theoretical analysis, adhering to the principles of both generalizability and flexibility.

The limitations of SOLO motivate future research on how to further unleash the potential of ultra-low-bit signed quantization in large-scale model training. According to the analysis in this paper, the signed EMA update is highly susceptible to the quantization errors due to the additional burden of sign representation and its direct impact on the update direction. Recent advances in sign gradient descent (Chen et al., 2024) may offer particular advantages in addressing this issue. Finally, although the superiority of SOLO has been demonstrated across various domains and training protocols, its effectiveness in large-scale model (e.g., 175B) pretraining remains unverified due to prohibitive computational costs. Conducting such an extensive evaluation would require the resources of a large AI research organization, which is beyond the scope of this study.

The prosperity of AI stems from the collective efforts of individual researchers within the community; however, the rapid scaling of model sizes is rendering fundamental research accessible only to those equipped with substantial computational infrastructure. There is an urgent need for affordable alternatives to reinvigorate research interest. SOLO advances this goal by slimming down the optimizer, which is the most memory-intensive part of the training process.

Appendix A Quantization Methods

In this part, we provide a detailed introduction to the aforementioned Linear and Dynamic Exponent (DE) quantization techniques. Particular emphasis is placed on the following mapping formulation, as it effectively unifies the majority of unsigned and signed quantization methods.

q=Q⁡(x):=argmink=02b−1⁡|xΔ−yk|.\displaystyle q=Q(x):=\mathop{\text{argmin}}\limits_{k=0}^{2^{b}-1}\big|\frac{x}{\Delta}-y_{k}\big|. (16)

Linear mapping represents one of the most widely adopted quantization methods due to its straightforward and practical implementation with levels evenly distributed over [0, 1] and [-1, 1]:

Unsigned:{0,12b−1,…,1};Signed:{0,±12b−1−1,…,±1}.\displaystyle\text{Unsigned:}\quad\{0,\frac{1}{2^{b}-1},\ldots,1\};\quad\quad\text{Signed:}\quad\{0,\pm\frac{1}{2^{b-1}-1},\ldots,\pm 1\}. (17)

The 4-bit Adam developed by Li et al. (2023a) observed a zero-point problem when applying the unsigned linear quantization to 2nd state update, yielding a slightly different variant of {12b,…,1}\{\frac{1}{2^{b}},\ldots,1\}.

Dynamic exponent mapping (Dettmers, 2015) places greater emphasis on handling both small and large magnitude values, as the received signals generally exhibit a non-uniform distribution. In the unsigned case, the bb bits are divided to serve three distinct functions:

b=E⏟exponent bits+1⏟indicator bit+F⏟fraction bits.b=\underbrace{E}_{\text{exponent bits}}+\underbrace{1}_{\text{indicator bit}}+\underbrace{F}_{\text{fraction bits}}. (18)

The leading zero bits EE represents the magnitude of the exponent. The subsequent indicator bit is the first bit set to one, signifying that all remaining bits are allocated for fraction representation. Then, a FF-bit linear quantization is performed over the range [0.1, 1]. Naturally, the first bit has to be reserved for the signed case. The 8-bit Adam developed by Dettmers et al. (2022) simplifies this quantization by removing the indicator bit. We illustrate the specific linear and DE mappings across b=2,3,4b=2,3,4 bits in Figure 7.

Denoted by rmin,rmedian,rmaxr_{\min},r_{\text{median}},r_{\max} the minimum, median, and maximum over all radii, it is easy to obtain the following fact:

B.2 Proof of Proposition 3.4

We first present a trivial lemma regarding a two-point distribution.

Lemma B.2.

Let XX be a random variable with

ℙ[X=a]=p,ℙ[X=b]=q=1−p.\mathbb{P}[X=a]=p,\quad\mathbb{P}[X=b]=q=1-p. (24)

Then, we have

𝔼⁡[X]=p​a+q​b,𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[X]=p​q​(a−b)2.\mathbb{E}[X]=pa+qb,\quad\mathbf{Var}[X]=pq(a-b)^{2}. (25)
Proof.

The proof is obvious. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.4.

For a yk−1≤x/Δ≤yky_{k-1}\leq x/\Delta\leq y_{k}, we have

1x^={Δyk−1,w.p.yk−x/Δyk−yk−1,Δyk,w.p.x/Δ−yk−1yk−yk−1.\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{x}}}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k-1}}},&w.p.\quad\frac{y_{k}-x/\Delta}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}},\\ \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k}}},&w.p.\quad\frac{x/\Delta-y_{k-1}}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}}.\end{array}\right.

Applying Lemma B.2 with p=yk−x/Δyk−yk−1,a=Δyk−1,b=Δykp=\frac{y_{k}-x/\Delta}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}},a=\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k-1}}},b=\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k}}}, we have

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(1x^)=(yk−x/Δ)​(x/Δ−yk−1)(yk−yk−1)2⋅(Δyk−1−Δyk)2.\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{x}}})=\frac{(y_{k}-x/\Delta)(x/\Delta-y_{k-1})}{(y_{k}-y_{k-1})^{2}}\cdot\Big(\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k-1}}}-\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{y_{k}}}\Big)^{2}.

The proof is finished by noting the fact that the magnitude of the first term is determined by the relative distance x/Δx/\Delta within the interval [yk−1,yk][y_{k-1},y_{k}]. ∎

B.3 Proof of Proposition 3.5

For an intermediate state value of qt=(βc)k+k′q_{t}=(\beta^{c})^{k+k^{\prime}}, the state transition probability after receiving a zero-value signal (zt+1=0z_{t+1}=0) can be represented as follows:

qt+1={(βc)k+k′,w.p.c−1c,(βc)k+k′+1,w.p.1c.q_{t+1}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(\beta^{c})^{k+k^{\prime}},&w.p.\quad\frac{c-1}{c},\\ (\beta^{c})^{k+k^{\prime}+1},&w.p.\quad\frac{1}{c}.\\ \end{array}\right. (26)

Thus, transitioning from the state value of (βc)k(\beta^{c})^{k} to (βc)k+s(\beta^{c})^{k+s} needs exact ss independent successes. Denoted by NN the counting of updates required to achieve exact ss successes, this random variable NN adheres to a negative binomial distribution with a success probability of 1/c1/c. It has been proved in the majority of standard statistical textbooks that

𝔼⁡[(βc)k→Ours(βc)k+s|z≡0]=𝔼⁡[N]=s1/c=c⋅s.\mathbb{E}\big[(\beta^{c})^{k}\xrightarrow{\text{Ours}}(\beta^{c})^{k+s}\big|z\equiv 0\big]=\mathbb{E}[N]=\frac{s}{1/c}=c\cdot s. (27)

B.4 Proof of Theorem 3.6

Revisting the quantized EMA update, we have

x^t+1\displaystyle\hat{x}_{t+1} =β⋅x~t+(1−β)⋅gt+1\displaystyle=\beta\cdot\tilde{x}_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot g_{t+1}
=β⋅(x^t+x~t−x^t)+(1−β)⋅gt+1\displaystyle=\beta\cdot(\hat{x}_{t}+\tilde{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{t})+(1-\beta)\cdot g_{t+1}
=β⋅x^t+(1−β)⋅(gt+1+β1−β​(x~t−x^t)⏟=:g~t+1).\displaystyle=\beta\cdot\hat{x}_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot\Big(\underbrace{g_{t+1}+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}(\tilde{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{t})}_{=:\tilde{g}_{t+1}}\Big).

Since standard stochastic rounding is applied independently in each update, the quantization error can be treated as noise within the gradient. Denote xt:=x^tx_{t}:=\hat{x}_{t}, yielding a standard EMA update:

xt+1←β⋅xt+(1−β)⋅g~t+1.\displaystyle x_{t+1}\leftarrow\beta\cdot x_{t}+(1-\beta)\cdot\tilde{g}_{t+1}.

𝔼⁡[g~t+1]=𝔼⁡[gt+1]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}_{t+1}]=\mathbb{E}[g_{t+1}] is obvious because of the zero expectation of quantization noise, and we are to establish its variance next, or equivalently

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[β1−β​(x~t−x^t)]=(β1−β​Δt)2​𝐕𝐚𝐫​[yqt−x^tΔt]=(β1−β​Δt)2​𝐕𝐚𝐫​[yqt].\mathbf{Var}\Big[\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}(\tilde{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{t})\Big]=\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}\mathbf{Var}[y_{q_{t}}-\frac{\hat{x}_{t}}{\Delta_{t}}]\\ =\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}\mathbf{Var}[y_{q_{t}}]. (28)

Without loss of generality, suppose yk−1≤x^t/Δt≤yky_{k-1}\leq\hat{x}_{t}/\Delta_{t}\leq y_{k}. It is easy to show that

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[yqt]=(yk−x/Δ)​(x/Δ−yk−1)(yk−yk−1)2⋅(yk−1−yk)2\mathbf{Var}[y_{q_{t}}]=\frac{(y_{k}-x/\Delta)(x/\Delta-y_{k-1})}{(y_{k}-y_{k-1})^{2}}\cdot(y_{k-1}-y_{k})^{2} (29)

by applying Lemma B.2 and noticing the fact that

yqt={yk−1,w.p.yk−x^t/Δtyk−yk−1,yk,w.p.x^t/Δt−yk−1yk−yk−1.y_{q_{t}}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}y_{k-1},&w.p.\quad\frac{y_{k}-\hat{x}_{t}/\Delta_{t}}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}},\\ y_{k},&w.p.\quad\frac{\hat{x}_{t}/\Delta_{t}-y_{k-1}}{y_{k}-y_{k-1}}.\end{array}\right.

Then, we have

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡[β1−β​(x~t−x^t)]\displaystyle\mathbf{Var}\Big[\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}(\tilde{x}_{t}-\hat{x}_{t})\Big] =(β1−β​Δt)2⋅(yk−x/Δ)​(x/Δ−yk−1)(yk−yk−1)2⋅(yk−1−yk)2\displaystyle=\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}\cdot\frac{(y_{k}-x/\Delta)(x/\Delta-y_{k-1})}{(y_{k}-y_{k-1})^{2}}\cdot(y_{k-1}-y_{k})^{2} (30)
≤(β1−β​Δt)2⋅14⋅(yk−1−yk)2\displaystyle\leq\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot(y_{k-1}-y_{k})^{2} (31)
⪅(β1−β​Δt)2⋅14⋅(2​rmax)2=(β1−β​rmax​Δt)2,\displaystyle\lessapprox\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot(2r_{\max})^{2}=\Big(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}r_{\max}\Delta_{t}\Big)^{2}, (32)

where the first inequality is because

p​q≤14if ​0≤p,q≤1​ and ​p+q=1,pq\leq\frac{1}{4}\quad\text{if }0\leq p,q\leq 1\text{ and }p+q=1,

and the second inequality holds true is due to the definition of rmaxr_{\max}.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Settings and Hyperparameters

Transformer-Base () on WMT’14. We consider the Neural Machine Translation (NMT) task follow the paper (Ott et al., 2018) and the codebase33 3 https://github.com/NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples/blob/master/PyTorch/Translation/Transformer . We train a Transformer-Base model on the WMT’14 English-German translation task from scratch. The specific setting can be found in Table 2. Four A800 GPUs have been used for the runs of tasks. We report the BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) results (averaged over 3 independent runs) from the best checkpoint.

RoBERTa-Large () on GLUE. NLP fine-tuning plays a critical role in achieving satisfactory performance across specific scenarios. During the early stages of NLP development, downstream tasks could not be effectively addressed using a single model, thus giving rise to various specialized domains, including Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Question Answering (QA), and Natural Language Generation (NLG). This study evaluates the performance of a low-bit optimizer in NLU44 4 https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/examples/pytorch/text-classification by fine-tuning the RoBERTa-L model (Liu, 2019) on the widely utilized GLUE benchmark (Wang et al., 2018a), which supports 8 different tasks. Their respective experimental settings are listed in Table 3. Besides, a linear schedule is employed for learning rate decay. With the exception of SST-2, which necessitates two GPUs for execution, the results on the remaining datasets are obtained using a single RTX 3090 GPU.

Swin-T () on ImageNet-1K. CV pretraining can provide a robust foundational model for a wide range of downstream tasks, among which image classification remains the most prevalent task for universal representation learning. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in computer vision applications, we train the tiny variant of the Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021) from scratch on the ImageNet-1K dataset (Deng et al., 2009) for the image classification task55 5 https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer . Detailed experimental configurations are provided in Table 4. The training is conducted using four NVIDIA V100 GPUs. For evaluation, we report both top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

DCN () on Criteo and HSTU-Large () on MovieLens. RS training has garnered greater interest from the industrial community compared to NLP and CV scenarios. Moreover, recommender systems are well-known for their large-scale user and item entities, resulting in massive embedding tables. This makes them particularly valuable for study in this context, as their ‘gigantic’ nature arises not merely from deeper or wider model architectures, but from the scale of the entities themselves. We consider two primary tasks across the recommendation pipeline. Sequential recommendation focuses on retrieving a list of candidate items to be passed to the subsequent ranking stage. Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction is a classical industrial application that estimates the probability of a candidate item being clicked. For the former, we adopt the recently proposed HSTU66 6 https://github.com/facebookresearch/generative-recommenders model (Zhai et al., 2024) on the widely used MovieLens-1M dataset, while for the latter, we consider the classic DCN77 7 https://github.com/MTandHJ/RecBoard/tree/master/DCN model (Wang et al., 2017) on the Criteo dataset. The hyperparameters can be found in Table 5.

LLaMA-7B () on Alpaca. LLM fine-tuning is one of the most compelling applications, but still faces challenges due to its high memory demands. Since ChatGPT’s pioneering days, a number of open source LLMs (Touvron et al., 2023; GenAI, 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024b) have been released, with the LLaMA series receiving the most attention. Hence, we fine-tune LLaMA-7B (Touvron et al., 2023) based on Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) codebase88 8 https://github.com/tatsu-lab/stanford_alpaca with the hyperparameters given in Table 6. Due to the utilization of three H800 GPUs for training, we adopt a total batch size of 120 instead of the standard 128, with 40 assigned to each GPU. For evaluation on the MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) and standard common sense reasoning benchmarks: ARC easy and challenge (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), and Social Interaction QA (Sap et al., 2019), we utlize OpenCompass (Contributors, 2023).

LLaVA-1.5 () visual instruction tuning. We follow the LLaVA-1.5 codebase99 9 https://github.com/haotian-liu/LLaVA to fine-tune the Vicuna-7B-v1.5 model (Chiang et al., 2023) on a mixed instruction tuning dataset comprising COCO (Caesar et al., 2018), GQA (Hudson & Manning, 2019), OCR-VQA (Mishra et al., 2019), TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019), and VisualGenome (Krishna et al., 2017). Due to the use of three H800 GPUs for training, we employ a total batch size of 120 instead of the standard 128 by assigning a batch size of 40 to each GPU. All other hyperparameters adhere to the recommended configurations and have been detailed in Table 7. In accordance with the official evaluation protocols, we assess the fine-tuned models on several benchmarks, including ScienceQA (Lu et al., 2022), TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019), POPE (Li et al., 2023c), and MME (Fu et al., 2023). Specifically, we report accuracy for ScienceQA and TextVQA; the F1-score averaged across the ‘Random’, ‘Adversarial’, and ‘Popular’ subtasks for POPE; the ‘Perception’ score for MME.
